title: FIRE Calculator: how it works, formula and examples
excerpt: FIRE Calculator: Your FIRE number (expenses × 25) and how many years until you reach it. Learn how to use it, the formula behind it, a worked example and…
content:
The [FIRE Calculator](/fire-calculator) is a free online tool on CalcHub. Your FIRE number (expenses × 25) and how many years until you reach it. Enter your annual expenses in retirement, already saved / invested, monthly contribution and annual return and the result appears straight away — no account or download needed. Because it runs entirely in your browser, the values you type never leave your device, and you can use it as often as you like.

Work out your FIRE number — the amount you need invested to retire early — and how long it will take to get there. The 4% rule says you can safely withdraw 4% of your investments a year, so your FIRE number is 25 times your annual expenses. This calculator uses that rule and your monthly contributions to estimate the years until financial independence. It is a projection, not financial advice: real returns vary, and the 4% rule is a rule of thumb, not a guarantee.

## How to use the FIRE Calculator

Start by entering your annual expenses in retirement ($), then entering your already saved / invested ($), entering your monthly contribution ($) and finally entering your annual return (%). The result updates as you type, so adjust any value and watch the answer change. If the answer is not what you expected, check the value you entered first — a missing digit or a wrong unit is the usual cause.

1. Enter what you expect to spend each year in retirement.
2. Enter what you have already saved and what you add each month.
3. Read your FIRE number and the estimated years to reach it.

## Formula

FIRE number = annual expenses × 25 (the 4% rule: 1 ÷ 0.04 = 25). Years to FIRE solves the compound-growth equation: target = saved × (1 + r)ⁿ + monthly × (((1 + r)ⁿ − 1) ÷ r), with the return applied monthly.

That is the standard formula for this calculation, and it is the same one the [FIRE Calculator](/fire-calculator) applies to the values you enter. You can work it out by hand, but the calculator is faster when you want to try several values, and it removes the risk of a slip in the arithmetic.

## Worked example

Here is a typical example. Spending $40,000 a year means a FIRE number of $1,000,000. Starting from $100,000 saved and adding $2,000 a month at 7% a year, you reach it in about 16.2 years — and $1,000,000 at 4% pays $3,333 a month. Try the same figures in the [FIRE Calculator](/fire-calculator) and you will get the same result — then change one value at a time to see how the answer moves.

## What the result shows

With the default values (Annual expenses in retirement: 40000 $, Already saved / invested: 100000 $, Monthly contribution: 2000 $, Annual return: 7 %), the [FIRE Calculator](/fire-calculator) returns Your FIRE number: $1,000,000, Years until FIRE: 16.2 years, Already saved: 10% of your FIRE number, Monthly income at FIRE (4% rule): $3,333.33 / month. The first figure is the headline result, and the rest break it down so you can see how the total is made up. If you want to compare with a related calculation, the [Loan Calculator](/loan-calculator) is worth a look before you finish.

## Where the 25× rule comes from

The 4% rule comes from the Trinity Study, which tested withdrawal rates against a century of US market data: withdrawing 4% of the starting balance a year (adjusted for inflation) survived 30-year retirements in almost every historical period. 25× expenses is the same rule rearranged — 1 ÷ 0.04 = 25. It assumes a mix of shares and bonds and a 30-year horizon; retiring at 40 needs the money to last longer, so many early retirees use 3.5% (about 28.6× expenses) instead.

## What the estimate leaves out

Taxes, fees, inflation, house purchases, children, and the fact that returns are lumpy — a crash early in retirement hurts far more than one late. The calculator also assumes you keep contributing the same amount every month and never withdraw. Treat the years-to-FIRE figure as a planning guide, and re-run it whenever your spending or savings change.

## Tips

A few things worth knowing before you rely on the result — most of them are about the numbers you put in, rather than the tool itself:

- Cutting expenses helps twice: it lowers your FIRE number and frees more to save.
- A higher savings rate matters far more than a slightly higher return.
- Re-run the numbers yearly — spending and markets both move.

## Frequently asked questions

### What is FIRE?

Financial Independence, Retire Early: saving and investing aggressively so your investments cover your living costs, letting you stop working — or work only on what you choose — years before normal retirement age. Try it with your own numbers in the [FIRE Calculator](/fire-calculator) — the result updates as you type, so you can test a few scenarios in seconds.

### How is the FIRE number calculated?

Annual expenses × 25. That comes from the 4% rule: if you withdraw 4% of your investments a year, $1,000,000 pays $40,000 a year. Try it with your own numbers in the [FIRE Calculator](/fire-calculator) — the result updates as you type, so you can test a few scenarios in seconds.

### Is the 4% rule safe?

It held up in almost every 30-year period in US market history, but it is a rule of thumb, not a guarantee. Longer retirements, high fees or retiring into a market crash all make it less safe — many early retirees plan on 3.5% instead. Try it with your own numbers in the [FIRE Calculator](/fire-calculator) — the result updates as you type, so you can test a few scenarios in seconds.

### What counts as annual expenses?

Everything you will spend in retirement: housing, food, transport, insurance, travel and fun. Be honest — underestimating spending is the most common FIRE mistake. Try it with your own numbers in the [FIRE Calculator](/fire-calculator) — the result updates as you type, so you can test a few scenarios in seconds.
